Day 3 · Finding (and Being) a Mentor in Business Analysis: Why Nobody Figures This Out Alone, and What to Do About It

How to Find and Approach a Mentor

A practical framework for identifying the right person and actually asking

By Tosin Ogunkoya · 2 September 2026 · 4 min read

Most people who say they never had a mentor never actually asked anyone. They assumed the answer would be no, or that reaching out uninvited was somehow inappropriate, and the assumption itself became the entire barrier, long before anyone had the chance to actually say no. This is worth stating plainly because it changes where the actual work is. The hard part of finding a mentor is rarely the asking itself, once you get there. It is getting past the internal story that the answer is already decided before you have tested it.

Find someone doing the specific thing, not just someone senior

The most common mistake is looking for the most senior or most impressive person available, rather than the person doing the specific thing you are actually trying to learn. A brilliant principal analyst at a huge consultancy may be a worse mentor for someone breaking into the field than a solid analyst two years further along who remembers exactly what that stretch felt like. Proximity to your actual next step matters more than seniority in the abstract.

The single biggest reason people avoid asking is imagining the ask as a large, open ended commitment, something close to "will you be my mentor," which understandably feels like a lot to request from someone you barely know. Nobody needs to agree to that up front, and asking for it that way makes a yes harder than it needs to be. The ask that actually works is small and specific: one conversation, thirty minutes, about one particular thing. Most ongoing mentoring relationships grow out of a first conversation that was never framed as mentorship at all. It simply went well enough that both people wanted to talk again.

Be specific about what you want to know

A vague request, something close to "can I pick your brain about business analysis," is genuinely harder to say yes to than a specific one, because it is unclear what is actually being asked for and how long it might take. Specificity does the opposite. It shows you have already done some thinking, and it lets the other person say yes quickly because they know exactly what they are agreeing to.

The actual script

A SPECIFIC, LOW-COMMITMENT ASK

You:

I've been following your work on stakeholder management and I'm early in my own BA career, trying to get better at exactly that. Would you have thirty minutes sometime in the next few weeks for me to ask a few specific questions about how you handle it? Happy to work around your schedule.

Notice what this message does. It names something specific and genuine, states clearly what is being asked for, bounds the time commitment, and puts the scheduling burden on you rather than them. That combination removes almost every reason to say no beyond genuinely not having the time.

What to do if the first person says no

A no is far more often about capacity than about you personally, and treating it as a referendum on your worth is the fastest way to stop asking altogether. Most people who say no to an ongoing mentoring relationship will still say yes to a single conversation, and most people who say no to any of it are simply overloaded at that specific moment, not making a judgment about whether you deserve their time.

RESPONDING WELL TO A NO

You:

Totally understand, thank you for being straight with me. If your schedule opens up down the line I'd still love thirty minutes, no pressure either way.

This keeps the door open without pressure, and it is worth simply asking someone else in the meantime rather than treating one no as evidence the whole approach does not work. It very often takes more than one attempt, and that is completely normal, not a signal you are doing something wrong.

Everything in this series so far argued that mentorship shortens the distance to real skill and real judgment. None of that value is reachable if the ask never happens. The framework above removes most of the actual friction, but the remaining friction, working up to sending the message, is something only you can close. Most people who eventually build a strong mentoring relationship describe the first ask as far less dramatic in hindsight than it felt in the moment before sending it.

Where to actually find these people

This is worth naming plainly, since the framework above assumes you already have someone in mind, and many people stall before that point. LinkedIn is the obvious starting place, particularly people who post genuinely useful content in the specific area you are trying to grow in, since writing publicly about a topic is itself a signal someone is willing to talk about it. Beyond that, look inside your own organisation first, since proximity and shared context make the first ask noticeably easier, and look at professional communities and alumni networks from any course or certification you have completed, since a shared credential gives you an immediate, legitimate reason to reach out that a cold message lacks. One more place worth checking, and often overlooked, is your own past. Former managers, former colleagues who moved further ahead, even an old lecturer or course instructor, already know your context and have already been shown some evidence of how you work, which lowers the barrier to a yes considerably compared to a stranger you are approaching cold. Rebuilding a dormant connection is very often easier than forming a brand new one from scratch.

Go out and be successful.
